Create a GPU-backed data frame

Source: R/tbl-gpu.R
tbl_gpu.Rd

cuplyr's GPU tables, called gibbles, live in GPU memory. gibble() is another name for tbl_gpu(). It transfers an R data frame to GPU memory using NVIDIA's libcudf library, enabling high-performance data manipulation operations. The resulting tbl_gpu object can be used with dplyr verbs like filter(), mutate(), select(), and collected back to R with collect().

Usage

tbl_gpu(data, ..., lazy = NULL)

gibble(data, ..., lazy = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'data.frame'
tbl_gpu(data, ..., lazy = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
tbl_gpu(data, ..., lazy = NULL)

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble to transfer to GPU memory. Supported column types include: numeric (double), integer, character, and logical.

...

Additional arguments passed to methods (currently unused).

lazy

Logical or character. Controls execution mode:

  • TRUE or "lazy" - Operations are deferred until collect()/compute()

  • FALSE or "eager" - Operations execute immediately

  • NULL (default) - Use the session option, then the environment variable, then the package default, which is lazy

The default can be changed with options(cuplyr.exec_mode = "eager") or the environment variable CUPLYR_EXEC_MODE=eager; the argument beats the option, which beats the variable. An invalid option value warns once and the default is used. All options are listed on cuplyr-options.

Value

A tbl_gpu object containing:

  • ptr - External pointer to the GPU table

  • schema - List with column names and types

  • lazy_ops - AST for pending operations (lazy mode only)

  • groups - Grouping variables

  • exec_mode - Execution mode ("lazy" or "eager")

Details

The data is immediately copied to GPU memory when tbl_gpu() is called (also in lazy mode; only the verbs are deferred). GPU memory is automatically freed when the R object is garbage collected.

Execution Modes

In lazy mode (the default), operations build an AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) that is optimized and executed only when collect() or compute() is called. This enables optimizations like:

  • Projection pruning (only load needed columns)

  • Mutate fusion (combine multiple mutates)

  • Filter reordering (cheapest filters first)

Errors in a verb's arguments (a missing column, a type error) are still raised when the verb is called. Printing a lazy table with pending operations (or calling glimpse() on it) runs the plan to show its first rows, under a # A gibble [lazy]: header; the table itself is unchanged and nothing is kept, so printing it twice runs the plan twice (compute() it first to look at it repeatedly). If the plan fails (an error, out of GPU memory), the print shows the schema and the message instead of raising.

In eager mode (lazy = FALSE), each dplyr verb executes immediately on the GPU. This is simple but can lead to unnecessary intermediate allocations.

For measured timings and memory use of the two modes, see vignette("performance", package = "cuplyr").

A vctrs::unspecified() column (all NA, no type yet) is stored as BOOL8. It collects back as vctrs::unspecified() only while it passes through filter(), arrange(), slice() and semi_join()/anti_join() (as a column of x, as in dplyr); every other verb (select(), mutate(), group_by() with computed expressions, slice_min()/slice_max(), a mutating join, vctrs::vec_slice()) returns it as a plain logical column. An unspecified column joined against a string, Date or factor key, or bound to a character column in bind_rows(), still errors.

Column type mappings from R to GPU:

  • numeric -> FLOAT64

  • integer -> INT32

  • character -> STRING

  • logical -> BOOL8

  • Date -> TIMESTAMP_DAYS

  • POSIXct -> TIMESTAMP_MICROSECONDS

Dates and times the GPU can't hold

A GPU Date holds whole days in an int32 and a POSIXct holds int64 microseconds. A value that doesn't fit becomes NA when it is uploaded, with a warning:

  • cuplyr_warning_infinite_timestamp: Inf or -Inf.

  • cuplyr_warning_timestamp_out_of_range: a finite value beyond about 5.8 million years either side of 1970 (Date) or 292,000 years (POSIXct).

Both also inherit cuplyr_warning_timestamp_unrepresentable, so one handler covers both. An upload raises at most one warning per class, listing every affected column with its count, e.g. `d` (2 values), `t` (1 value). NA and NaN are ordinary missing values and never warn. The same applies to every other way values reach the GPU: copy = TRUE joins, bind_rows(), $<-, a constant in mutate(), and the result of a verb that ran on the CPU. A fractional Date is floored with its own warning, cuplyr_warning_fractional_date.

Gibbles

"Gibble" is the user-facing name of a tbl_gpu: print() starts with # A gibble: and the dimensions, and gibble(), as_gibble() and is_gibble() are aliases of tbl_gpu(), as_tbl_gpu() and is_tbl_gpu(). The class stays tbl_gpu, and tbl_sum() still returns dplyr's values.

The CRAN package gibble (geometry decomposition, Michael Sumner) also exports a function called gibble(). When both packages are attached, the one attached last masks the other; cuplyr::gibble() always works.

See also

collect.tbl_gpu to transfer data back to R, compute.tbl_gpu to execute and keep on GPU, filter.tbl_gpu, mutate.tbl_gpu, select.tbl_gpu for data manipulation

Examples

library(dplyr)
if (has_gpu()) {
  # Transfer mtcars to GPU (lazy by default)
  gpu_mtcars <- tbl_gpu(mtcars)
  print(gpu_mtcars)

  # Operations are deferred until collect()
  result <- tbl_gpu(mtcars) |>
    filter(mpg > 20) |>
    mutate(kpl = mpg * 0.425) |>
    collect()

  # Eager mode: each verb runs at once
  eager_tbl <- tbl_gpu(mtcars, lazy = FALSE)

  # Or make every new table eager:
  # options(cuplyr.exec_mode = "eager")
}
#> # A gibble: 32 × 11
#> $ mpg  <dbl> 21, 21, 22.8, 21.4, 18.7, 18.1, 14.3, 24.4, 22.8, 19.2
#> $ cyl  <dbl> 6, 6, 4, 6, 8, 6, 8, 4, 4, 6
#> $ disp <dbl> 160, 160, 108, 258, 360, 225, 360, 146.7, 140.8, 167.6

#> $ drat <dbl> 3.9, 3.9, 3.85, 3.08, 3.15, 2.76, 3.21, 3.69, 3.92, 3.92
